people.name: U Thant
body: On 3 November 1961, after the death of Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld, the UN General Assembly appointed a Burmese ambassador as Acting Secretary-General to fill the rest of his term. U Thant, a former schoolteacher from the Irrawaddy delta town of Pantanaw, took charge of the world body in New York during the Cold War. U is a Burmese honorific, not a first name.

Thant was born in Pantanaw on 22 January 1909. He studied at the National High School there and at University College, Rangoon, then went back to the school as a teacher. After placing first in the Anglo-Vernacular Secondary Teachership Examination, he became its headmaster in 1931, and he led it again for about four years from 1943. After World War II, as Burma moved toward independence from Britain, he joined the government. He was Press Director in 1947, Director of Broadcasting in 1948 and Secretary to the Ministry of Information in 1949. In 1953 he became Secretary for projects in the Prime Minister's Office, and in 1955 he also took on the post of Executive Secretary of the Economic and Social Board.

In 1957 he went to New York as Burma's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, with the rank of ambassador. He was Vice-President of the General Assembly in 1959 and chaired the UN Congo Conciliation Commission in 1961. After his acting appointment he was formally named Secretary-General on 30 November 1962 and reappointed on 2 December 1966 for a term that ended on 31 December 1971.

He died of cancer on 25 November 1974, after a long illness, at age 65. His body lay in state at UN Headquarters in New York for 24 hours before it was flown home to Burma. His grandson, the historian Thant Myint-U, was born in New York and grew up in his household.
keyFacts: 22 January 1909: Born in Pantanaw, Burma.
1931: Became headmaster of the National High School, Pantanaw.
1957–1961: Burma's Permanent Representative to the UN.
3 November 1961: Appointed Acting UN Secretary-General.
30 November 1962: Appointed Secretary-General; reappointed 2 December 1966; term ended 31 December 1971.
25 November 1974: Died of cancer; lay in state at UN Headquarters.

people.name: Thant Myint-U
body: Thant Myint-U grew up in New York in the home of his maternal grandfather, UN Secretary-General U Thant. He was born in New York City on 31 January 1966 to parents of Burmese descent, and he became one of the best-known English-language writers on Burma's history for American readers.

He studied at Harvard, graduating in the late 1980s, at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, and at Cambridge, where he earned a Ph.D. in history in 1996. He worked on UN peacekeeping operations in Cambodia (1992–93) and the former Yugoslavia (1994–96), including as the UN's spokesman in Sarajevo during the Bosnian War, and from 2000 to 2007 at the UN Secretariat in New York.

His books include The Making of Modern Burma, The River of Lost Footsteps (2006), Where China Meets India (2011) and The Hidden History of Burma (2019). In September 2025 he published Peacemaker, a biography of his grandfather.

He later worked in Myanmar itself. In 2012 he was appointed to the country's National Economic and Social Advisory Council and, that same year, founded and chaired the Yangon Heritage Trust, which works to protect the city's historic architecture. In 2015 he received the Grand Prize of Japan's Fukuoka Prize, and in 2018 India's Padma Shri. As of October 2026, his official biography lists him as chairman of U Thant House in Yangon and a senior fellow of the United Nations Foundation, and says he was elected an Honorary Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, in 2024.
keyFacts: 31 January 1966: Born in New York City.
1996: Ph.D. in history, Cambridge.
2006: The River of Lost Footsteps.
2012: Founded the Yangon Heritage Trust.
2015: Fukuoka Prize (Grand Prize).
2025: Peacemaker, a biography of U Thant.

people.name: Wakar Uddin
body: In February 2018, students at the University of Connecticut gathered for an awareness dinner on the Rohingya crisis, hosted by the Bangladeshi Student Association with the Pakistani Community at UConn and the Muslim Students Association. Their keynote speaker was a Penn State professor who was himself Rohingya: Wakar Uddin.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority from Arakan (Rakhine) State in western Burma. Many have fled to Bangladesh, Malaysia and, in smaller numbers, the United States.

Uddin was born in Maungdaw, in Arakan State. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees in integrated pest management at the University of Nevada and a doctorate in plant pathology at the University of Georgia in 1996, and worked at Georgia's Plant Disease Clinic. In 1998 he joined Penn State as a turfgrass pathologist, later becoming a professor of plant pathology and turfgrass disease specialist.

Alongside his science, he was the founding chairman of the Burmese Rohingya Association of North America, president of Muslim Aid America, and Director General of the Arakan Rohingya Union, which Penn State describes as a federation of 61 Rohingya organizations worldwide. He spoke to American audiences, from universities to faith and media networks, about what was happening to Rohingya people. He died on 29 April 2022.
keyFacts: Born in Maungdaw, Arakan (Rakhine) State, Burma.
1996: Ph.D. in plant pathology, University of Georgia.
1998: Joined Penn State, later professor of plant pathology.
Founding chairman, Burmese Rohingya Association of North America.
Director General, Arakan Rohingya Union.

people.name: Elaisa Vahnie
body: In 1996, after he faced arrest for taking part in Burma's pro-democracy movement, Elaisa Vahnie, a Chin leader from Chin State, left the country and went to India. That journey eventually led to Indiana.

With a U.S. Department of State scholarship, he studied at Indiana University and earned a bachelor's degree in 2006. He then spent two years in Malaysia as an International UN Volunteer Specialist with the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, working on refugee protection and resettlement. There he helped sponsor a policy giving all ethnic groups from Burma equal access to protection, and pressed for faster resettlement to third countries. He returned to Indiana University for a master's degree in public affairs.

In 2011 he and other community members co-founded the Burmese American Community Institute in Indianapolis. As of October 2026, its leadership page names him President and CEO. On 17 January 2025, at the Indiana Statehouse, the Indiana Civil Rights Commission gave him its Martin Luther King Jr. Humanitarian Award. The International Center also profiled him in its 50 for 50 series, marking its 50th anniversary, on people and groups who helped make Indiana a global hub.
keyFacts: 1996: Left Burma after facing arrest for pro-democracy activity; went to India.
2006: Bachelor's degree, Indiana University, on a State Department scholarship.
Two years with the UN refugee agency in Malaysia.
2011: Co-founded the Burmese American Community Institute, Indianapolis.
17 January 2025: Indiana Civil Rights Commission MLK Humanitarian Award.

people.name: Wendy Law-Yone
body: In 1967, a young woman in Rangoon tried to leave Burma to rejoin her husband abroad. She was caught and held for two weeks before being released. Her father, Edward Law-Yone, a newspaper publisher and editor, had been imprisoned after the military took power in 1962. Years later Wendy Law-Yone turned her family's experience of dictatorship and exile into fiction.

She was born in Mandalay on 1 April 1947 and raised in Rangoon. She came to the United States in 1973, attended college in Florida, graduating in 1975, and settled in Washington, D.C. She worked as a writer and published in the Washington Post.

Her first novel, The Coffin Tree (Knopf, 1983), follows a young woman from Burma who arrives in New York. Irrawaddy Tango followed in 1993. She received a National Endowment for the Arts literature award in 1987.

In 2002 she received the David T.K. Wong Creative Writing Fellowship at the University of East Anglia in England. Her novel The Road to Wanting (2010) was longlisted for the Orange Prize in 2011. Golden Parasol (2013) is a memoir of her father and her family.
keyFacts: 1 April 1947: Born in Mandalay, Burma; raised in Rangoon.
1962: Her father, a newspaper publisher, was imprisoned under military rule.
1973: Moved to the United States.
1983: The Coffin Tree.
1987: National Endowment for the Arts literature award.
2010: The Road to Wanting, longlisted for the Orange Prize in 2011.

people.name: Hre Mang
body: In November 2022, voters in Perry Township on the south side of Indianapolis chose three people from seven at-large candidates for their school board. One of them was Hre Mang, a pastor from the Chin community. WTHR 13News reported the result under the headline "First Burmese-American elected to school board."

Mang is pastor of Falam Christian Church of Indianapolis. Falam is a town in Chin State, in western Burma. He has also taught as an adjunct professor at Crossroads Bible College. He holds a bachelor's degree in theology from Grace Bible College in India and a master's degree in public affairs from Indiana University. He is a founding member of the Chin Community of Indiana, a social services organization.

Perry's board members serve four-year terms, and the district lists his term as running through December 2026. As of October 2026, Chalkbeat reports that he is not seeking re-election. Three of the seven seats are on the ballot on 3 November 2026.

Founding member, Chin Community of Indiana.

people.name: Bryant Y. Yang
body: In November 2020, Governor Gavin Newsom appointed a federal prosecutor named Bryant Yang to the Los Angeles County Superior Court. The American Bar Foundation called it a historic appointment, saying Yang was the first Burmese American judge in the United States.

Yang, then 38 and living in Arcadia, filled the seat left by the retirement of Judge Yvonne T. Sanchez. He earned his law degree at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law. He was an associate at Morrison & Foerster from 2007 to 2010, a special prosecutor and special counsel for the Burbank and Glendale city attorneys in 2010, a clerk for the Ninth Circuit and a federal district court from 2010 to 2012, and deputy director of voter protection for Organizing for America–Nevada in 2012. He practiced at Irell & Manella from 2012 to 2016. From 2016 he was an Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California.

He served as president of the Asian Pacific American Bar Association of Los Angeles County in 2016. He helped Asian American and Pacific Islander lawyers seek judicial appointments and created a Judgment Enforcement Clinic to help people collect on court judgments. He also spent time on the Myanmar-Thailand border working with refugees from Burma.
keyFacts: J.D., UC Berkeley School of Law.
2016: President, Asian Pacific American Bar Association of Los Angeles County.
2016–2020: Assistant U.S. Attorney, Central District of California.
13 November 2020: Appointed to the Los Angeles County Superior Court.
Described by the American Bar Foundation as the first Burmese American judge in the U.S.

people.name: Myo Myint
body: In 1988, as huge pro-democracy protests filled Rangoon, a disabled former soldier stood before a crowd of about 8,000 people. Myo Myint had been badly wounded by an explosion while serving in Burma's army and lost a leg and much of the use of his hands. WBOI describes a mortar setting off mines while he worked as a minesweeper; Radio Free Asia's 2011 profile gives other details, including an eye. He urged soldiers not to turn on their own people, and, according to Radio Free Asia, about 200 of them joined the protests. That speech led to his arrest.

He had joined the army at 17, in 1980, following his father into military service. After the 1988 crackdown he spent nearly 15 years in prison, much of it in solitary confinement, and he turned down offers of early release in exchange for keeping silent. He was released in 2004 and, facing new threats, fled to a refugee camp on the Thai border, where he stayed four years. There the Irish photojournalist Nic Dunlop found and interviewed him.

In 2008 he was resettled in Fort Wayne, Indiana, where relatives already lived. He worked with refugee groups including Amani Family Services and Catholic Charities, often as an interpreter. He taught English as a second language, co-produced a weekly public television program for the community from Burma and helped edit a monthly magazine. He wrote for Burmese publications, recorded for Radio Free Asia, and spoke before the Refugee Congress and at the State Department in Washington.

Dunlop made a documentary about his life, Burma Soldier, which HBO released in May 2011. He married Karen Bender, a Catholic Charities social worker who had been his first contact in Fort Wayne. He died in February 2026, at age 63. Local public radio reported that he kept a jar of soil from Burma in his home until he died.
keyFacts: 1980: Joined the Burmese army at 17.
1988: Spoke at a Rangoon pro-democracy rally; arrested.
2004: Released after nearly 15 years in prison; fled to the Thai border.
2008: Resettled in Fort Wayne, Indiana.
May 2011: HBO documentary Burma Soldier released.
February 2026: Died at 63.

people.name: Aung San Suu Kyi
body: On 19 September 2012, in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol, members of Congress gathered to present the Congressional Gold Medal to Daw Aung San Suu Kyi of Burma. Congress had passed the legislation four years earlier, while she was held under house arrest. She had chosen to wait so that she could accept the medal in person.

She was born in Rangoon on 19 June 1945, the daughter of Aung San, the leader of Burma's independence movement, and Khin Kyi. She studied politics at Delhi University in 1960 and earned a B.A. at St Hugh's College, Oxford, from 1964 to 1967. From 1969 to 1971 she worked at the UN Secretariat in New York. In 1972 she married the British scholar Michael Aris.

In 1988 she returned to Burma to care for her mother just as the mass pro-democracy uprising began. She became general secretary of the National League for Democracy, formed that September. On 20 July 1989 the military placed her under house arrest. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991, and by her release on 13 November 2010 she had spent about 15 years under house arrest.

In 2012 the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum gave her its first Elie Wiesel Award. Her party won the 2015 election, and she became State Counsellor, Burma's de facto leader. When the military launched a campaign against the Rohingya, she did not condemn or stop it, and in 2019 she defended Burma against genocide allegations at the International Court of Justice. In March 2018 the Museum rescinded her award, citing her failure to stop the campaign.

On 1 February 2021 the military seized power and detained her. A junta court's sentences reached 33 years by 30 December 2022, later commuted to 27. On 30 April 2026 the military announced that amnesty reductions had left her with about 18 years to serve, and that she would serve them at a home instead of in prison, at a location it did not disclose. As of October 2026, authorities say she is under house arrest in Naypyidaw. Her son Kim Aris spoke with her by phone on 22 October 2026, their first direct conversation since the coup, and an ASEAN envoy who visited that month ended her trip with no public meeting with her.
keyFacts: 19 June 1945: Born in Rangoon, daughter of independence leader Aung San.
1991: Nobel Peace Prize.
19 September 2012: Received the Congressional Gold Medal in the Capitol Rotunda.
March 2018: U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum rescinded its 2012 Elie Wiesel Award.
1 February 2021: Detained in the military coup.
30 April 2026: Moved from prison to house arrest, by the military's announcement.
people.connectToWork: Her story is admired and disputed. How do you keep from bringing up a public figure, or a country's politics, as if everyone from that country shares one view?

people.name: Michael Aung-Thwin
body: In 2018 the National University of Singapore named a University of Hawaiʻi professor to its George E. Bogaars endowed professorship for 2018–2019, to teach Myanmar's history and give a public lecture. Michael Aung-Thwin had spent decades in American universities teaching the deep past of the country where he was born.

He was born in Yangon (Rangoon), Burma, in 1946. He went to high school at Kodaikanal International School in South India, then came to the United States for college. He earned a B.A. at Doane College in Nebraska, an M.A. at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and a Ph.D. at the University of Michigan.

His teaching took him to Elmira College, Kyoto University, Northern Illinois University and the National University of Singapore. He settled at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where he worked in the Center for Southeast Asian Studies and became Emeritus Professor of Asian History.

His books include Pagan: The Origins of Modern Burma (1985), The Mists of Ramanna (2005), A History of Myanmar Since Ancient Times (2013) and Myanmar in the Fifteenth Century (2017). He died after a long illness on 14 August 2021 at his home in Hawaiʻi. His son, Maitrii Aung-Thwin, is also a historian of Southeast Asia. His family asked for donations in his memory to the Burma Studies Foundation.
keyFacts: 1946: Born in Yangon (Rangoon), Burma.
B.A., Doane College; M.A., University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Ph.D., University of Michigan.
1985: Pagan: The Origins of Modern Burma.
2013: A History of Myanmar Since Ancient Times.
2018–2019: George E. Bogaars endowed professor, National University of Singapore.
14 August 2021: Died in Hawaiʻi.

people.name: MiMi Aung
body: On 19 April 2021, a small helicopter called Ingenuity lifted off the surface of Mars. It was the first powered, controlled flight by an aircraft on another planet. The project manager who had led its team was MiMi Aung, a Burmese American engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.

She was born in Illinois in 1968. Her parents had met in the United States while earning doctorates. Coconuts Yangon describes her mother, Hla Hla Sein, as the first Burmese woman to earn a doctorate in mathematics at a U.S. university. The family returned to Burma when she was a young child, at 11 she moved to a school in Malaysia, and at 16 she came back to the United States.

She earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1988 and a master's in 1990. That year she joined JPL, where she spent more than three decades, beginning with signal processing for NASA's Deep Space Network and moving into guidance, navigation, control and autonomous systems.

She led the Mars helicopter project from the mid-2010s. Ingenuity rode to Mars attached to the Perseverance rover and was meant to make only a few test flights; by March 2022 it had flown 20 times. In 2021 she left JPL for Amazon's Project Kuiper, a satellite internet program, as a director of program management, and TIME named her one of its 100 most influential people. In February 2022 she was elected to the National Academy of Engineering.
keyFacts: 1968: Born in Illinois to Burmese parents who both held doctorates.
1988 and 1990: B.S. and M.S. in electrical engineering, University of Illinois.
1990: Joined NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
19 April 2021: Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet.
February 2022: Elected to the National Academy of Engineering.
people.connectToWork: Her family moved between Burma, Malaysia and the U.S. What does your intake ask about a person's schooling and moves, and what does it assume instead?

people.name: Alex Wagner
body: In April 2018, the television journalist Alex Wagner published a book that began with a question she had carried since childhood: who are my people, and where am I from? Futureface followed her mother's family back to Burma and her father's family to Luxembourg and Iowa.

Wagner's mother is a Burmese immigrant. Wagner graduated from Brown University in 1999, where she studied art history. From 2011 to 2015 she hosted her own program on MSNBC. She then contributed to The Atlantic and CBS News, and in 2018 became a co-host of Showtime's political documentary series The Circus.

In August 2022 she returned to MSNBC to host Alex Wagner Tonight at 9 p.m. MSNBC canceled the show in early 2025; the Asian American Journalists Association noted that it had been one of the few national news programs anchored by Asian Americans. She stayed on as a senior political analyst, and as of September 2026 she was appearing as a political analyst on MS NOW, the network's new name.

Futureface took its title from a 1993 Time cover about the changing face of America. In it she explores her mother's stories of leaving home, her family's history in Burma and the limits of DNA ancestry tests.

2011–2015: Host of her own MSNBC program.

August 2022: Began hosting Alex Wagner Tonight on MSNBC; canceled early 2025.
September 2026: Political analyst on MS NOW.

people.name: Rich Cho
body: In 2010, the Portland Trail Blazers named a new general manager. Rich Cho, born in Burma, became the first Asian American general manager in the NBA and, according to the league, in any American major professional sport.

Cho was not yet three when his family left Burma in 1968; his father, a journalist, had criticized the military government. A church in Fort Wayne, Indiana, sponsored them, and after several years they settled in Federal Way, Washington. He earned a mechanical engineering degree at Washington State University and worked as an engineer at Boeing in Seattle from 1989 to 1994.

While studying law at Pepperdine University, he interned with the Seattle SuperSonics, and he stayed in basketball. He was assistant general manager for about ten years with the SuperSonics and, after the team moved, the Oklahoma City Thunder.

After one season in Portland, he became general manager of the Charlotte Bobcats, later the Hornets, in 2011 and led that front office until 2018. In April 2019 the Memphis Grizzlies hired him as Vice President of Basketball Strategy.

Engineering degree, Washington State University; engineer at Boeing, 1989–94.
Law degree, Pepperdine University.
2010: General manager, Portland Trail Blazers.
2011–2018: General manager, Charlotte Bobcats and Hornets.
April 2019: Vice President of Basketball Strategy, Memphis Grizzlies.

people.name: Miemie Winn Byrd
body: Miemie Winn Byrd, a Burmese American retired U.S. Army officer, served as a civil affairs officer and economic advisor and, on several U.S. delegations and operations, as a linguist and cultural advisor.

She earned a bachelor's degree in economics and accounting at Claremont McKenna College, an MBA at the University of Hawaiʻi and a doctorate in education leadership at the University of Southern California.

She built two careers at once: 16 years in auditing, accounting and financial management at multinational companies and a Silicon Valley start-up, and 28 years in the U.S. Army, retiring as a lieutenant colonel. At U.S. Pacific Command she was Deputy Economic Advisor, Civil-Military Operations Plans Officer and Interagency Operations Officer, and from 2003 to 2007 she edited its Asia-Pacific Economic Update.

She joined the Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies in Honolulu in 2007 and, as of October 2026, is listed there as a professor. Her expertise covers security in Myanmar and Southeast Asia, economic security and leadership. In 2013, at the request of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, she led the effort to establish the Suu Foundation, a U.S. nonprofit.

B.A., Claremont McKenna College; MBA, University of Hawaiʻi; Ed.D., University of Southern California.
28 years in the U.S. Army; retired as a lieutenant colonel.

people.name: Joshua Van
body: On 6 December 2025, at UFC 323 in Las Vegas, a 24-year-old fighter from Houston won the UFC flyweight championship when champion Alexandre Pantoja was injured 26 seconds into the bout. Joshua Van, born in Myanmar, defended the title against Tatsuro Taira at UFC 328 in May 2026, and on 19 September 2026, at UFC 331 in Los Angeles, he beat Pantoja again by unanimous decision.
He was born on 10 October 2001 in Hakha, the capital of Chin State in western Burma, and is based in Houston, Texas.

He made his UFC debut on 24 June 2023 at UFC on ABC 5 in Jacksonville, Florida, beating Zhalgas Zhumagulov by decision on short notice. Afterward the 21-year-old said the cage "felt like home." After UFC 331 his professional record stood at 18 wins and 2 losses, 11–1 in the UFC.

people.name: Nay Lin Soe
body: Nay Lin Soe is a disability rights advocate from Yangon whose training profile lists a physical disability from polio. He completed the Duskin Leadership Training in Japan, an independent-living course for people with disabilities from Asia-Pacific countries. In May 2011 he and other people with disabilities founded the Myanmar Independent Living Initiative in Yangon, where he served as program director and later as executive director.

At a 2019 forum in Tokyo, he described how his organization and others helped shape Myanmar's ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2011, the 2015 disability rights law, and changes that improved disability access in elections. He also said that there were no personal assistance services in the country, so family members usually did that work, and that good laws had not yet changed daily life because budgets were lacking.

In 2016 the International Foundation for Electoral Systems gave him its Charles T. Manatt Democracy Award in Washington, D.C., for that work, including accessible elections. He lives in Myanmar, not the U.S., and no dated account of his work after 2019 was found.

people.name: Myo Min Htet
body: Myo Min Htet, from Yangon, took part in the 20th Duskin Leadership Training in Japan. He uses a manual wheelchair. He says the work of former trainees who lead the Myanmar Independent Living Initiative inspired him to apply.

In his final report he wrote that barriers in Myanmar start "from our doorstep, at our own home." He also wrote that he had believed people with severe disabilities would be "incapable of making their own decisions", and that seeing independent living in Japan changed that view. He planned to press government agencies on accessibility, develop a barrier-free smartphone app and open an independent-living counseling center.

In a later report looking toward 2025, he signs as a Senior Officer in Business Sustainability at ATOM Myanmar. He describes helping arrange a donation of braille embossers and paper to the Myanmar Christian Fellowship of the Blind, and taking part in an employment fair where ATOM showed job openings for persons with disabilities.
keyFacts: Born 29 October 1998, by his training profile; from Yangon.

institutions.name: Center for Burma Studies, Northern Illinois University
institutions.type: Scholarly center, museum collection and archive
institutions.location: Pottenger House, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, Illinois
body: In 1986 the Burma Studies Group of the Association for Asian Studies chose Northern Illinois University to be the national Center for Burma Studies. At the same time scholars created the Burma Studies Foundation to collect Burmese materials. The center opened with an inauguration ceremony on 29 July 1987. Its first director was NIU art historian Richard Cooler, a specialist in Burmese art.

It collects and preserves information and objects from the peoples and cultures of Burma/Myanmar and makes them available. It does not grant degrees. Its collections include Burmese art, music recordings, manuscripts, maps, photographs, oral histories and personal papers. In 2015 it lent objects to the Asia Society in New York for the exhibition Buddhist Art of Myanmar.

It publishes the Journal of Burma Studies and the Bulletin of the Burma Studies Group, hosts the International Burma Studies Conference, teaches Burmese language courses and does outreach to schools and communities.
keyFacts: 1986: Selected as the national Center for Burma Studies.
29 July 1987: Inauguration ceremony.

institutions.name: Burmese American Community Institute
institutions.type: Community organization, education and social services
body: In 2011, community members in Indianapolis, among them former democracy activist and UN refugee agency worker Elaisa Vahnie, founded the Burmese American Community Institute. It describes itself as a nonprofit serving the Burmese and immigrant community of greater Indianapolis.

Its site lists an Upward College Program, summer programs, a Civic and Cultural Education Program, immigration and legal services, civic participation and community engagement, employment and microenterprise work, community health and wellness, and a Myanmar Initiative. The organization says it has assisted more than 25,000 people since it began. That figure is its own and has no outside count behind it.
As of October 2026, its leadership page names Elaisa Vahnie President and CEO, and its news page carries 2026 posts. No Minnesota office for it could be found.

institutions.name: Burma Superstar
body: Burma Superstar opened on Clement Street in San Francisco's Inner Richmond district in the early 1990s. By The Bold Italic's account, its first owner, Taik Wu, and his family had hoped to build a popular Burmese restaurant, but business was slow. Around 2000 it was taken over by Desmond Tan, who was born in Yangon and moved to the Richmond District at age 11, and his partner Joycelyn Lee. 7x7 dates the takeover to 2000 and The Bold Italic to 1999, and The Bold Italic calls him Desmond Htunlin. Michelin reports that they bought it because their favorite Burmese restaurant was closing.

Its tea leaf salad, its rainbow salad of 22 ingredients and its mohinga, a catfish noodle soup, became its best-known dishes, and lines out the door became part of its reputation. It was included in the first Michelin Guide to San Francisco in 2007.

The business grew to include East Bay locations and a sister restaurant, Burma Love. In March 2017 Ten Speed Press published Burma Superstar, a cookbook written by Tan with Kate Leahy. As of October 2026, the restaurant's own site still calls Clement Street the original location.
keyFacts: Early 1990s: Opened on Clement Street.
2007: Included in the first Michelin Guide San Francisco.

institutions.name: Myanmar Independent Living Initiative
body: People with disabilities founded the Myanmar Independent Living Initiative in Yangon on 8 May 2011 to start an independent-living movement in Myanmar. It registered with the Ministry of Home Affairs that September. Its motto is "We are agents of change."

It offers rights-based disability training to government, nonprofit, religious, business, professional and media groups, and it runs national essay, poem, cartoon, painting and speech competitions on disability. It aims to serve people with all types of disability, prioritizing women, children and people with severe disabilities.

In 2019 its executive director, Nay Lin Soe, reported 28 local branches, 54 employees and 4,752 disabled members. Those are the organization's own numbers. He also said it worked with businesses on employment and helped shape national laws. No dated account of its work after the 2021 military coup was found. It is not a Minnesota resource.
keyFacts: 8 May 2011: Founded in Yangon.
Led by people with disabilities; covers all types of disability.
Trains religious and community groups as well as government.
institutions.connectToWork: If a family assumes disability rights came from the U.S. system, or a provider does, what would change if they knew Myanmar's disabled people have led their own movement?

institutions.name: Ethnic Minorities of Burma Advocacy and Resource Center
institutions.location: Des Moines, Iowa, with programs across the state
body: Seven community advocates from ethnic organizations and the local advocacy community founded the center in 2012, after Karenni, Karen, Chin, Shan, Mon and Rakhine refugees from Burma began resettling in Iowa in 2008 and 2009. It calls itself Iowa's first refugee-led service provider. Its site lists language helplines, education, interpretation, crisis and advocacy services, a parent navigator and a community pantry.

Its leaders, Director Abigail Sui and Executive Director Henny Ohr, are listed on a training deck about culture and mental health among refugees from Burma, hosted by Iowa's Department of Health and Human Services. The deck covers the trauma of flight, the stresses of resettlement, stigma, traditional healing and service barriers. It recommends trained interpreters for the correct language and dialect, bicultural workers, support for the whole family, and trust built through community leaders. It closes with slides in Burmese, Karen, Falam Chin and Karenni.
Its site does not list disability-specific services.
keyFacts: 2012: Founded by seven community advocates.
Serves refugees from Burma across Iowa.
Services include interpretation and a parent navigator.
institutions.connectToWork: This is a nearby example of refugee-led work with health and human services. What would have to be true at your agency for a partnership like that to hold real money and real decisions?

disability.intro:
This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, people from Burma means many ethnic groups, languages and faiths, including Bamar, Chin, Kachin, Karenni, Mon and Rohingya people. Experiences differ by generation, region, education and years spent in camps or in countries such as Malaysia or India.

No Minnesota study of how people from Burma understand disability was found, and nothing specific to Chin, Kachin, Karenni, Mon or Rohingya people. What follows draws on one qualitative study in Yangon, an Iowa refugee organization's training deck on mental health, an Australian account of one family, a U.K. charity's blog and the words of disability advocates in Myanmar. The Karen page has its own section.
questions: What language, and which dialect, do you prefer for this meeting?
How would you describe what you notice about yourself or your family member? What words do you use for it?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped, or got in the way?
What would you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family or community would you like to be part of decisions?
What has helped so far, from family, church, temple, mosque or healers? How would you like those to fit into a plan?
Is there anything you are worried others might hear about? Would you rather not use an interpreter you know?
If you are the person who gives most of the care, how are you doing yourself?
What would you like to know about how this service works, and about whether it has anything to do with police or immigration?
Would you like this in writing, in your language, or would you rather talk it through?

context.heading: What sources have reported about explanations
body: Hannah Ware and Matthew Schuelka interviewed 22 people in Yangon in May 2015: 13 teachers at two private English-medium schools (8 Buddhist, 3 Christian, 2 Muslim) and 9 others, including an elder monk and staff of disabled people's organizations. The authors call it an illustrative case study, not a representative sample. Teachers described disability in medical terms and through the Buddhist idea of karma. One repeated a saying her mother used, roughly "if you do bad things you need to pay for it." The authors report that this was often not said as a judgment, and some teachers linked understanding a cause to a "calming mind."

A 2019 blog post by the U.K. charity HART says that a belief about karma and rebirth underlies stigma in Burma and sustains an acceptance that suffering is necessary. A 2025 account from Aspect, an Australian autism service, tells the story of one refugee mother from Burma and adds the service's own general claims: that some Buddhists link disability to karma and turn first to healers, that some Christians see spirit possession or divine punishment, and that some people blame diet in pregnancy or poor parenting. Neither source gives a sample. Ask how the person understands what is happening. None of this tells you what they think.

sources.label: Ware and Schuelka, Disability & Society (2019), author version
HART UK, Karma, Rebirth and Disability (29 May 2019)
Aspect, A refugee mother's path to empowerment and understanding (4 November 2025)

context.heading: Mental health, stigma and getting to services
body: EMBARC's training deck, hosted by Iowa HHS and undated (its latest references are from 2021), is about mental health among refugees from Burma in Iowa, not disability broadly. It gives no study sample. It lists these expectations: be stoic, bear problems without complaint, consult religious leaders, receive care from family, and seek encouragement from family, friends and community leaders. It says mental health problems are tied to taboos and treated as a private family issue, and that spirit possession is thought to be one cause, addressed through ceremonies or purification rituals.

The barriers it names are mostly about systems: treatment that does not respond to beliefs, providers who decline refugee referrals or lack experience with trauma, long waits, insurance and eligibility problems, missing or unqualified interpreters, transportation, and poor care coordination. It also names fear and mistrust of police and limited knowledge of U.S. health, school and legal systems. Before reading a missed visit as culture, check these first.

Its suggestions are direct referral and appointment scheduling, case management, support for the whole family, translated materials, trained interpreters, bicultural workers, and trust built through family or ethnic community leaders.

sources.label: EMBARC, Culture and Mental Health Among Refugees from Burma, hosted by Iowa HHS

context.heading: Mothers, family care and faith
body: Aspect says blame for a child's disability often falls on the mother and harms her mental health, and that families may hide a diagnosis for fear of gossip and shame. The mother in its account was helped by a migrant resource center, by therapists and by a new church that welcomed her son, whom she came to call "a gift from God." She asked for "listening kindly" from professionals. HART, citing the UN, says women and girls with disabilities face double discrimination and a higher risk of gender-based violence.

Nay Lin Soe told a 2019 forum that Myanmar had no personal assistance services and that family members usually do that work. A family may be doing a great deal and may never have been offered paid support at home, so explain what exists and ask what they would want. Involve a pastor, monk or other leader only with the person's consent.

sources.label: Aspect, A refugee mother's path to empowerment and understanding (4 November 2025)
HART UK, Karma, Rebirth and Disability (29 May 2019)
Nay Lin Soe, Presentation for Myanmar (2019)

context.heading: Rights and disabled leaders in Myanmar
body: Disabled people's organizations in Myanmar promote rights and independent living, and they pressed for the 2011 ratification of the UN disability convention and the 2015 disability rights law, by Nay Lin Soe's account. Do not assume a family holds any one view. He also said that people still tend to see disability through charity and medicine, that nationwide data are not available, and that good laws had not changed daily life because budgets were lacking.

He cited the 2014 census for 4.6 percent of the population, about 2.3 million people, having a disability, and a 2010 government survey finding that one in two had never attended school. Those are his figures, from before the 2021 coup, and he said himself that the data are limited. Use them as background on one country at one time, not as a measure of anyone in Minnesota.

sources.label: Nay Lin Soe, Presentation for Myanmar (2019)
Duskin Leadership Training in Japan, Introduction to the Myanmar Independent Living Initiative

context.heading: Language and words for disability
body: EMBARC stresses getting the correct language and dialect; Burmese is not always the right choice. Aspect says Burmese has no specific word for autism, and EMBARC says there is often no word or term for mental illness, so people may use phrases such as "thinking too much" or "heavy heart", or describe specific symptoms. Expect a description before a label.

Ware and Schuelka report that newer, more enabling Burmese words exist, including ones that translate as "differently abled", but that disabling language is probably still more common. They also note that people of other faiths may use the same words without the Buddhist meaning. No reliable list of Burmese disability terms could be checked, so none is offered here. Ask a trained interpreter or the person which words they use and prefer, and do not invent translations.

communityRoutes.name: Karen Organization of Minnesota, Caregivers Program
communityRoutes.purpose: Listed among the social services of an organization that says it works with Karen, Karenni, Mon and other refugees from Burma. It supports in-home caregivers of adults over 60 or adults with neurological dysfunction, with counseling, training, support groups, temporary substitute care and transportation. The coordinator is Hta Thi Yu Moo, 651-202-3107. Ask who can take part and in which languages.

organizations.intro: This list covers people from Burma other than Karen people, who have their own page. The Karen Organization of Minnesota says more than 3,000 refugees from other ethnic groups in Burma live in the state, and estimates 2,000 to 5,000 Karenni and 1,000 Mon, alongside more than 20,000 Karen. Other counts differ: The Catholic Spirit reported about 12,000 Karenni in 2017, attributing that to the same organization, and Sahan Journal said in 2025 that some estimates double the 2,000 figure. These are estimates, not a census. No Chin, Kachin or Burmese Muslim institution in Minnesota was found. A Carleton College project documented a Burmese Buddhist monastery, Sitagu Dhamma Vihara, in Maplewood and its move to Chisago City in 2014, but nothing dated since could be found, so it is not listed. Democratic Voice of Burma reported in May 2025 that the Burmese service of Voice of America had gone silent that March, and no new dated reporting was found on its site, so it is not listed either. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts. Ask people what they follow.
